It does however, provide power to many other systems.
INTRODUCTIONM

An aircraft's safety of flight depends on a well designed power distribution system. Power distribution systems must be designed to ensure critical aircraft systems are always available, even in an emergency situation.
In this lesson we will look at the operation of a basic power distribution system. Knowing how a power distribution system works will help in the effective troubleshooting of a faulty system.

LESSON MENU
BASIC POWER DISTRIBUTION

One of the most important systems on an aircraft is the power distribution system. The power distribution system is used to transfer power from a multitude of sources to any device on the aircraft requiring power.
DISCUSSION

Examples of power sources would be; a battery, DC alternators, DC starter generators, AC alternators, and external power. A battery is used only to start the engine and in emergency situations. External power can only be used when a plane is on the ground.

All power sources are connected to a bus bar. A bus bar is a simple copper bar capable of handling all of the power being transferred throughout the system. Between the power sources and the bus there are protective devices.

These protective devices include relays, current limiters, and switches. In the case of generators and alternators, current limiters are used to disconnect them from the bus if a problem occurs that could result in damage or undesired effects on the bus.

For external power, a relay is used to make sure that power is attached to the aircraft properly. If power isn't connected properly, the relay won't allow the external power to be connected to the bus.

Relays also are used to keep power flowing in one direction. The Reverse Current Relay (RCR) prevents battery or external power from flowing towards the alternator when the alternator is idle.ernator.
Once the alternator is producing enough power, the RCR closes and connects the alternator to the main bus.. Remember, a diode allows current flow in one direction, but not the other.

A master switch is provided to disconnect power from the bus. On some aircraft this may only disconnect the battery, and on others, both the battery and the generators. If the generators are not controlled by the master switch, they will have individual switches to disconnect them.

Another important component of the power distribution system is the ammeter. An ammeter will indicate to a pilot how much power an alternator is producing. This is important when power is limited and loads need to be removed to boost the output of the generators.

Some ammeters don't need to be monitored by the pilot. In automatic systems, current sensing devices determine if too much power is being used on the bus. Different relays will disconnect different loads automatically based on their importance to flight.............

This importance of loads is known as Load Hierarchy. This means when systems are designed, essential loads are placed on the bus system in places where faults are least likely to occur. This makes disconnecting non-essential loads much easier.

The unit that controls the bus is called the bus power control unit. There are many different control and monitoring units that feed into the bus power control unit. These units are constantly monitored to provide complete uninterrupted power.

BASIC POWER DISTRIBUTION OP
In this experiment, you will look at the operation of a basic power distribution system. By understanding this operation, troubleshooting of a faulty system can be quick and effective.
EXPERIMENT
The circuits are mounted on two circuit cards. The controls, components and indicators represent different sections of an aircraft power distribution system.
The PC130-735 card is the AC to DC generator system. This card will provide two balanced DC voltages. For this experiment, we will only be concerned with one of them...
The trainer will simulate the generator outputs. Inside a generator AC voltage is produced which is converted to a pulsating DC waveform using diodes and capacitors.
This output from the generator will be directed to the Voltage Regulator circuit. This circuit will adjust the output voltage level of the generator and balance the voltage.

The balance adjusts the difference between the two voltage outputs. Both outputs should be exactly the same to provide correct current flow. We will be balancing the two voltages, but again only using one of them.
Switches S1 and S2 are used to turn on and off the output of the generators. The output we will be using is 12 volts DC.
The PC130-734 card is the basic power distribution card. Pick it up and examine it.
To the left of the bus are the inputs and controls to the power distribution system. For this system we have an alternator input, generator 1 from PC130-735, and a simulated battery input.
There are four indicators and two switches in this area of the card. Two LEDs are used to indicate if power is being applied from its associated source.
The other two LEDs are used to indicate the status of the aircraft's engine. This is important because this engine powers the alternator (generator) that we are using.
S2 is used to start the engine and S1 is used to control all bus input power. With this switch off, the entire power to the aircraft is off.

On the right side of the bus there are two sections; protection circuits and loads. The protection circuits, circuit breakers, are used to prevent a faulty load from altering power delivered to other sections of the aircraft.
The loads just represent arbitrary loads that would be seen on an aircraft. The LEDs located within the load illustrations indicate if power is being applied to them.

MEASUREMENT SETUP - Press and release the S2 start button.
When you pressed the start button, the starter turned on to start the engine. Releasing the button disengaged the starter. Since the alternator is now generating power it powers the bus.

If you measured the alternator voltage (TP1 to ground) and the battery voltage (TP1 to TP5) before pressing the start button, you may have noticed that the alternator voltage is approximately 3 V more than the battery voltage. This is so the alternator power can power the bus and charge the battery at the same time.
At this point, the power distribution system is working properly. Let's cause the alternator to fail and see what happens to the system.
What happened to the power applied to the bus?
The alternator continued to supply power.
Neither sources supply the bus with power.
When the alternator cut off, the battery should have begun to power the bus. Check your setup or ask your instructor for assistance.
TRY AGAIN!
It is important for the battery to supply power to the bus when all other sources are disabled. If the battery didn't supply power no power would be available in the aircraft.
Most batteries can supply necessary power for about an half hour. This gives pilots a chance to land or fix the problem. Without any power, the aircraft would become non-operational in flight.
Let's say we were able to get the alternator working again. Since battery power is limited, let's reconnect it to the bus and see what happens.

The alternator has been reconnected to the bus. As you can see, power to the bus is now delivered from the alternator. It is important to note that the an actual aircraft battery would be recharging again.
The last thing that we are going to look at is circuit protection. It is very important that faulty loads are isolated from the bus.
If you had a faulty load that shorted voltage to ground, all other loads would not operate and the power source may become damaged.
To be certain that loads can be isolated from the bus, a circuit breaker is used. When a load becomes faulty the circuit breaker actually disconnects it from the bus.
Let's create a faulty load on the bus and observe the operation of the circuit breaker.
You should have observed circuit breaker one pop-out and the instrument panel light turn off. At this point the instrument panel has been isolated from the bus.
Let's say we have fixed the fault in the instrument panel. To reconnect power you need to reset the circuit breaker. For this particular model just push in the red button until it locks.
You should observe that the instrument panel light is now on. If a load is critical and needed for flight, being able to reconnect it to the system is important, provided it can be fixed.
Let's create another fault on the bus and determine which load is malfunctioning. tch to ON.........................................
Which load has a fault and has been isolated from the bus?
The second circuit breaker should have popped out. The component faulted is the component connected to this circuit breaker, cabin lights. Check your setup or ask your instructor for assistance....
TRY AGAIN!

Assume that you have fixed your cabin lights and that you are ready to attach them to the bus. Press the red button that is extending from the second circuit breaker. The four lights should illuminate.......
As you can see, there are many important sections to a basic power distribution system. While the actual structure of a system may be different, its basic operation is the same.
Without the proper knowledge of a basic bus system, troubleshooting can be time consuming and costly.
